A pundit points to today's most famous college dropouts who built billion-dollar companies (Gates, Zuckerberg, etc.) and concludes that dropping out of college to pursue a startup is, in general, a statistically sound path to success. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The flaw is that Gates and Zuckerberg actually finished their degrees
There is no flaw — the examples are real companies, so the conclusion is statistically valid
The flaw is that billion-dollar companies are evenly distributed between dropouts and graduates, so the comparison is meaningless
Survivorship bias — the reasoning only looks at the rare successful survivors while ignoring the vastly larger number of dropouts whose startups failed

questions.q: A talented rookie wins 'Rookie of the Year' after an outstanding debut season — likely an unusually good season even relative to their true underlying skill level. Pure statistics predicts their following season's performance will typically be:
choices: Closer to their long-run average skill level — i.e., somewhat worse than the outstanding rookie season, simply due to regression to the mean
Even better than the rookie season, since the player is clearly improving and trending upward
There is no statistical reason to expect any change at all, since past performance guarantees future results
Exactly identical to the rookie season, since skill level alone fully determines performance

questions.q: Game A, played alone, is a losing game over time (the odds slightly favor the house). Game B, played alone, is also a losing game over time. Yet by alternating between A and B — even just switching randomly each round — the combined strategy becomes, on average, a WINNING game. What does this result, known as Parrondo's paradox, demonstrate?
choices: This only works because the 'losing' games were already secretly profitable on their own
Any sequence of losing games will always remain a losing game in total, with no exceptions
The games must have been miscalculated — two losing games can never combine into a winning one
Combining two individually losing strategies can produce a winning strategy, because switching between them changes the underlying dynamics in a way neither game alone exhibits

questions.q: Philosopher Edmund Gettier described cases where a person has a belief that is both true and backed by seemingly adequate justification, yet almost all philosophers agree the person does not actually 'know' the fact — because pure luck, not the justification itself, is what connects the belief to the truth. What does this show about the classical definition of knowledge as 'justified true belief'?
choices: It shows that true beliefs can never be justified, so the definition is incoherent from the start
Justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge — some justified true beliefs are true merely by luck, not knowledge
It shows that justification is irrelevant to knowledge, and only truth matters
It shows that justified true belief is both necessary and perfectly sufficient for knowledge, with no exceptions

questions.q: You bought a $200 non-refundable, non-transferable concert ticket. The day of the show, you feel ill and know attending will be miserable, with no benefit beyond the music itself. Purely in terms of maximizing your well-being from this point forward, should the fact that you already spent $200 affect your decision to attend?
choices: No — but only because concert tickets specifically don't count as sunk costs
Yes — you should go, because skipping would double your financial loss
Yes — you should go, because otherwise the $200 is wasted
No — the $200 is already gone regardless of your choice (a sunk cost), so it is irrelevant to a rational decision based only on future costs and benefits

questions.q: Die A beats Die B more often (over many rolls), and Die B beats Die C more often. Must Die A also beat Die C more often, the way ordinary comparisons (like 5 > 3 > 1) transitively guarantee 5 > 1?
choices: No — 'beats more often' need not be transitive for dice; nontransitive dice exist where C can beat A
Only if all three dice are standard six-sided dice
It's impossible to construct dice where this fails
Yes, beats-more-often is always transitive, just like ordinary number comparisons

questions.q: You have a coin that lands heads with some unknown, possibly biased probability p, and you want to simulate a perfectly fair 50/50 coin flip. Von Neumann's trick: flip it twice; if the two results differ, use the first flip as your fair result; if they match, discard both and repeat. Why is this exactly fair for any p strictly between 0 and 1?
choices: P(heads,tails) = p(1−p) exactly equals P(tails,heads) = (1−p)p, so conditional on a differing pair, each order is equally likely regardless of p
Because flipping any coin twice always averages out its bias
Because discarding matching pairs removes the coin's bias from future flips too
Because p(1−p) is always exactly 0.5 for any value of p

questions.q: A patient whose health is borderline is reclassified from the 'healthy' group into the 'sick' group, with no actual change in anyone's health. Since that patient was the least healthy of the healthy group and becomes the healthiest member of the sick group, what happens to the average health of the two groups (the Will Rogers phenomenon)?
choices: Only the healthy group's average goes up; the sick group's average falls
Both groups' average health goes up, even though nobody actually got healthier
Only the sick group's average goes up; the healthy group's average falls
Neither average can change unless someone's actual health changes
